How often do professional players scan?

In a study of 27 players from one Premier League club, players made about 0.44 scans per second in the seconds before they received the ball, a little under one look every two seconds. Central midfielders and centre backs scanned the most, forwards the least, and everyone scanned less under heavy pressure.

  • More scanning, slightly better passing. In the same study, players who scanned more before receiving had a slightly higher chance of completing their next pass. The authors call it a small but positive effect (Jordet et al., 2020).
  • Pros scan more than amateurs. Using Premier League player-cam footage, Geir Jordet's team compared 118 Premier League players with Dutch amateur players. The professionals scanned significantly more, and Frank Lampard and Steven Gerrard were the top two (Sky Sports, 2021).
  • A scan is a snapshot. An eye-tracking study of four elite midfielders in real 11 v 11 matches found their eyes settled on one spot in only 2.3% of scans, and they saw more opponents than teammates when they looked (Aksum et al., 2021).

That last point is why this test only gives you 3 seconds or less. In a match you don't stare at the picture. You glance, and your brain has to keep enough from that glance to choose your first touch.

How else is scanning tested?

Scanning is tested in five main ways: counting head turns on match video, eye-tracking glasses, passing tests on the pitch where targets can be behind you, VR headset drills, and screen tests like this one. Each method measures a different part of scanning, so treat any single score as one piece of the picture.

MethodWhat it measuresWho uses itCan you do it yourself?
Scan count on match videoHow often you turn your head before you receiveResearchers and analysts, counted by hand from videoYes, if someone films you with a wide view
Eye-tracking glassesWhere your eyes land during each scanResearch studiesNo, it needs lab equipment
Passing test with targets behind youPasses per minute when you must check 120, 180 or 360 degrees around youResearchers testing pro playersA simple version, with one friend (see below)
VR headset drillsHow often and when you look in a virtual gameVR apps such as Be Your Best (from $19 a month billed annually, checked October 2026)Yes, with a Meta Quest headset
Screen recall test (this page)How much you keep from one short lookUnscouted, freeYes, right now

The passing test is the newest. In a 2025 study, players from the first and reserve teams of two professional clubs in Ghana did three passing tests. Their average score dropped as more targets moved behind them: about 30 passes per minute at 120 degrees, 27 at 180 degrees and 26 at 360 degrees. First-team players scored higher than reserves, and better scores went with better results in 3 v 1 rondos (Hunter et al., 2025, Biomechanics).

Can you do a scanning test on the pitch?

Yes. With a wall, a ball and one friend you can run a 2-minute scanning check: your friend shows fingers behind you while the ball comes back off the wall, and you call the number before your first touch. Count how many you get right out of 20 and repeat the same setup every week.

  1. Set up. Stand 6 metres from a wall. Your friend stands about 4 metres behind you.
  2. Pass. Play the ball against the wall. As soon as it leaves your foot, your friend moves to your left or right and holds up 1 to 5 fingers.
  3. Look and call. Check your shoulder and shout the number before your first touch. A call after your touch counts as a miss.
  4. Score it. 20 passes, one point per correct call. Write the score down with the date.
  5. Make it harder. Return the ball first time, so you have to look earlier. Or your friend steps in on an even number and you turn away from him.

This is our own practice check, not a research test, so there is no official "good" score. Its value is the comparison: same wall, same distances, same friend, week after week. Do the screen test above on the same day and you train both halves, taking the look and keeping the picture.

How can I improve my scanning?

Look with a question in mind: is someone on me, where is the free player, which side is open. Then build the habit in training with a shoulder check before every pass you receive, and name one thing you saw.

How can I improve my scanning?

Look with a question in mind: is someone on me, where is the free player, which side is open. Then build the habit in training with a shoulder check before every pass you receive, and name one thing you saw.

How many times per second do pro footballers scan?

In one study of a Premier League club, players averaged about 0.44 scans per second before receiving the ball, a little under one look every two seconds. Central midfielders and centre backs scanned the most and forwards the least.

Why does the test only show the picture for 2 seconds?

Because real scans are quick. You turn your head, take a snapshot and look back at the ball. An eye-tracking study of elite midfielders found their eyes settled on one spot in only 2.3% of scans, so a short look is normal.

Can I test my scanning without a screen?

Yes. Pass against a wall while a friend stands behind you and holds up fingers as the ball travels back. Call the number before your first touch, score yourself out of 20 and repeat the same setup each week to compare.

Who are the best scanners in football?

In Geir Jordet's research on Premier League player-cam footage, Frank Lampard and Steven Gerrard were the top two scanners among 118 players. A 2021 Sky Sports interview with Jordet also singled out Kevin De Bruyne as a master at scanning.
